'''Bruce Raymond Voeller''' (May 12, 1934 – February 13, 1994) was a [[biologist]] and researcher, primarily in the field of [[AIDS]], and [[gay rights]] activist. In 1973 he co-founded the [[National Gay and Lesbian Task Force|National Gay Task Force]]. In 1977, the now renamed [[National LGBTQ Task Force]] held the first-ever meeting at the [[White House]] with President [[Jimmy Carter]] marking the first time openly gay and [[lesbian]] leaders were welcomed there, and the first official discussion of [[Gay and lesbian rights movement|gay and lesbian rights]] in the White House. Within the [[Timeline of HIV/AIDS|first few years]] of the [[AIDS pandemic]] Voeller coined the term ''acquired immune deficiency syndrome'' (AIDS) which we use to this day.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.glbtqarchive.com/ssh/voeller_b_S.pdf|title=Voeller, Bruce (1934-1994)|date=2015|website=glbtq Encyclopedia|access-date=2019-08-22}}</ref>

==Early life and education ==
Voeller was born in [[Minneapolis]] and raised in [[Oregon]].<ref name=nytimes>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/24/obituaries/dr-bruce-voeller-is-dead-at-59-helped-lead-fight-against-aids.html |title=Dr. Bruce Voeller Is Dead at 59; Helped Lead Fight Against AIDS |first=Wolfgang |last=Saxon |date=1994-02-24 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref> When he was at school, he was assured by a school counselor that he was not homosexual, even though he had felt such feelings very early on.<ref name=stewart>{{cite book |title=Gay and Lesbian Issues |url=https://archive.org/details/gaylesbianissues00stew |url-access=limited |first=Chuck |last=Stewart |publisher=ABC-CLIO |year=2003 |isbn=1-85109-372-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gaylesbianissues00stew/page/n180 168]–9}}</ref>

Voeller graduated with a bachelor's degree from [[Reed College]] in 1956.<ref name=stewart /> He was awarded a five-year fellowship to the [[Rockefeller University|Rockefeller Institute]],<ref name=nytimes /> and earned a [[Ph.D.]] in biology in 1961.<ref name=stewart />

== Career ==
Voeller became an associate professor at the Rockefeller Institute in 1966. His research interest was in the fields of phytocytology and [[plant physiology]]. He wrote four books while there, as well as editing others' work, and writing numerous papers and articles.<ref>{{cite journal|title=A new cytoplasmic component of plant cells|year=1963|pmc=2106312|last1=Bonneville|first1=M. A.|last2=Voeller|first2=B. R.|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|volume=18|issue=3|pages=703–708|doi=10.1083/jcb.18.3.703|pmid=14064120}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.143.3604.373|title=Gibberellins: Their Effect on Antheridium Formation in Fern Gametophytes|year=1964|doi=10.1126/science.143.3604.373|last1=Voeller|first1=B. R.|journal=Science|volume=143|issue=3604|pages=373–375|pmid=17821060|bibcode=1964Sci...143..373V|s2cid=28754286|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Induction of fern spore germination|year=1969|pmc=223310|last1=Weinberg|first1=E. S.|last2=Voeller|first2=B. R.|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|volume=64|issue=3|pages=835–842|doi=10.1073/pnas.64.3.835|pmid=16591804|bibcode=1969PNAS...64..835W|doi-access=free}}</ref> He married Kytja Scott Voeller,<ref name="nytimes" /> whom he met at graduate school, and they had three children.<ref name="stewart" />

He [[Coming out|came out]] at the age of 29,<ref name="nytimes" /> and divorced from his wife in 1971. After becoming president of the New York [[Gay Activists Alliance]], he decided it was not wide enough in its coverage. Therefore, with some friends, he founded the  [[National Gay and Lesbian Task Force|National Gay Task Force]] in October 1973, and was its director until 1978. The Task Force established affiliations with more than 2000 gay groups, and by 1978 had over 10,000 members.<ref name="stewart" /> In 1977, the National Gay Task Force (now the [[National LGBTQ Task Force]]) successfully initiated the first-ever meeting between the [[White House]] and more than a dozen gay and lesbian leaders. President [[Jimmy Carter]]’s assistant, [[Midge Costanza]], met with Task Force co-chairs and board members as well as representatives of gay and lesbian organizations for a briefing on critical policy issues affecting this constituency. The meeting marked the first time openly gay and lesbian leaders were welcomed at the White House and the first official discussion of [[Gay and lesbian rights movement|gay and lesbian rights]] in the White House.  Attendees at the White House meeting included: [[Frank Kameny]], Myra Keddell, Charles Brydon, Ray Hartman, Betty Powell, [[William B. Kelley|William Kelley]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.glhalloffame.org/index.pl?item=9&todo=view_item|title=William B. Kelley|access-date=2015-05-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150703204422/http://www.glhalloffame.org/index.pl?item=9&todo=view_item|archive-date=2015-07-03|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Troy Perry]], [[Jean O'Leary]], [[Elaine Noble]], George Raya and Pokey Anderson.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thetaskforce.org/press/releases/prAPC_032207 |title=Today marks 30th anniversary of first-ever meeting between White House and gay leaders |publisher=TaskForce |date=2007-03-26 |access-date=2013-11-01 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131103014614/http://www.thetaskforce.org/press/releases/prAPC_032207 |archive-date=2013-11-03 }}</ref> He also founded the Mariposa Foundation, which specializes in [[sex research]], and [[Sexually-Transmitted Diseases|sexually transmitted diseases]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bnl.gov/bera/activities/globe/bruce_voeller.htm |title=Bruce Voeller |publisher=bnl.gov |access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref>

In 1973, Bruce Voeller, as president of the Gay Activists Alliance, complained to [[Jack Paar]] and ABC about remarks and terminology that the organization regarded as derogatory toward gay people. Paar subsequently invited Voeller and fellow GAA members [[Arnie Kantrowitz]] and Nathalie Rockhill to appear on the March 8 broadcast of ''[[Jack Paar Tonite]]''.<ref name="Richman1973">{{cite news
|last=Richman
|first=Vicki
|title=Jack Paar to Host GAA on March 8th
|work=Gay
|volume=4
|issue=97
|date=March 12, 1973
|pages=1, 4
|url=https://www.houstonlgbthistory.org/Houston80s/Assorted%20Pubs/GAY/Gay-4-97-19730312.pdf
|access-date=July 11, 2026
}}</ref> The discussion became contentious as Paar defended some of his language and views about homosexuality, while the activists challenged anti-gay terminology and stereotypes.<ref name="Humm2022">{{cite news
|last=Humm
|first=Andy
|title=Arnie Kantrowitz, Gay Pioneer, Author, Professor, and Lover, Dies at 81
|work=Gay City News
|date=January 24, 2022
|url=https://gaycitynews.com/arnie-kantrowitz-gay-pioneer-author-professor-and-lover-dies-at-81/
|access-date=July 11, 2026
}}</ref>

In the early 1980s, [[AIDS]] was known by various names, including GRIDD ([[Gay-related immune deficiency|Gay Related Immune Defense Disorder]]). Because this term was inaccurate, Voeller coined the term ''acquired immune deficiency syndrome''.<ref name="stewart" /> His partner was Richard Lucik, who was also his associate at Mariposa. Voeller died in 1994 of an AIDS related illness in [[California]], at the age of 59.<ref name="nytimes" />

In June 2019, Voeller was one of the inaugural fifty American “pioneers, trailblazers, and heroes” inducted on the [[National LGBTQ Wall of Honor]] within the [[Stonewall National Monument]] (SNM) in [[New York City]]’s [[Stonewall Inn]].<ref name=":23">{{Cite web|url=https://www.metro.us/news/local-news/new-york/stonewall-inn-lgbtq-wall-honor|title=National LGBTQ Wall of Honor unveiled at Stonewall Inn|last=Glasses-Baker|first=Becca|date=June 27, 2019|website=www.metro.us|access-date=2019-06-28|archive-date=2019-06-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190628133313/https://www.metro.us/news/local-news/new-york/stonewall-inn-lgbtq-wall-honor|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="SDGLN">{{Cite web |last=Rawles |first=Timothy |date=2019-06-19 |title=National LGBTQ Wall of Honor to be unveiled at historic Stonewall Inn |url=https://sdgln.com/news/2019/06/19/national-lgbtq-wall-honor-be-unveiled-historic-stonewall-inn |access-date=2019-06-21 |website=San Diego Gay and Lesbian News |language=en}}</ref> The SNM is the first [[National monument (United States)|U.S. national monument]] dedicated to [[LGBT rights in the United States|LGBTQ rights]] and [[History of LGBT people|history]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ebar.com/news/news//272833|title=Groups seek names for Stonewall 50 honor wall|website=The Bay Area Reporter / B.A.R. Inc.|language=en|access-date=2019-05-24}}</ref> while The Wall's unveiling was timed to take place during the [[Stonewall 50 – WorldPride NYC 2019|50th anniversary]] of the [[Stonewall riots]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sfbaytimes.com/stonewall-50/|title=Stonewall 50|date=2019-04-03|website=San Francisco Bay Times|access-date=2019-05-25}}</ref>
